name: AAAFlow Studio
tagline: Type a script in, a finished YouTube video comes out. Fully local, one GPU, zero cloud.
note: Built end to end with Claude Fable. I used up my entire Claude Fable allowance on this one project, and this is what came out of it: a studio that runs four YouTube channels off one gaming GPU.
summary: AAAFlow is a local-first video studio that turns a written script, or just an idea, into a finished, human-looking YouTube video on a single machine: an RTX 5060 Ti with 16 GB of VRAM, no cloud calls at all. It runs a strict voice-first pipeline (the whole script is narrated in one take, and everything else is timed to that narration) and operates four channels, each with its own niche, art direction, designed narrator voice, brand identity and YouTube account. Six videos have been produced with it, about 25 minutes of finished footage across 370 composed scenes, from 3-minute stories to a 10-minute, 141-scene documentary, and two of them are public on YouTube right now. The bar is simple: if a viewer or a platform can tell it was AI-generated, that is a failure.
problem: Most AI video tools produce obvious, formulaic output and lean on the cloud. AAAFlow aims for the opposite: broadcast-quality, human-looking videos produced end to end on one consumer GPU, driven entirely by a script, with every stage tuned to remove the tells that give AI video away, and every published critique turned into a permanent system fix rather than a one-off patch.
role: Solo builder. Architecture, pipeline, model integration, and the full UI.

highlights: Runs entirely on one RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB with zero cloud calls. A single job queue serializes TTS, image, video and music models, and engines load lazily and auto-unload so nothing fights over VRAM.
Voice first: the whole script is narrated in one take, humanized, then Whisper aligns every scene to that voice, so all timing flows from the narration.
Four channels, one machine: each channel is a folder with its own niche, look, designed voice, brand kit, SEO pool and YouTube account.

Channels can be born by STUDYING a reference channel: the study intake ranks its uploads, evidence packs measure its style shot by shot, and the findings distill into skill packs a new channel is generated from.
A deterministic auto-director plus one editable 'effects grammar' dictionary decide every transition, sound and emphasis, so even a weak script yields a competently edited video.
Text is never burned into frames: Wan renders content, Remotion typesets all on-screen text, and a vision-model glyph guard re-rolls any clip that leaks letters.
Every critique becomes a system change, never a one-off fix: no phantom hands or mirrors, clothed figures enforced in code, a flat natural narrator, endings that settle instead of stop.
Ships like a product: research-driven SEO, eight typeset thumbnail templates, vertical Shorts, scheduled private-first uploads, and live YouTube-side status with drift detection.

sections.heading: The four channels
sections.body:
Every channel is its own studio: a folder holding its niche, art direction, designed voice, pipeline defaults, brand kit and YouTube credentials. The app opens on a hub of channel cards; entering one scopes everything to that channel.

- Main, 'the whole studio, one channel': five original seed channels merged into one everything-channel, carrying the earliest proven defaults and the first produced video (a con-artist story about the man who sold the Eiffel Tower).
- The Midnight Menagerie, 'every exhibit was real': true-macabre stories presented as a dark-carnival sideshow. Its ten-slot visual identity (profile, banner, thumbnail models, characters, ambiance) is rendered by the studio's own brand generator from a fixed ComfyUI node graph, and its narrator is a designed voice with a performance arc that begins curious and settles as the story closes. Ships with a VHS filter and an ember color grade. Three videos, including a 10-minute, 141-scene documentary; two of them are public on YouTube right now (@MidnightManagerie, linked above).
- Unruly History, 'the past, behaving badly': extreme true history told as deadpan hand-inked comic storytelling, with its own faster-paced voice design.
- Fathom, 'true stories, properly investigated': born differently. A reference documentary channel was STUDIED: the study intake pulled its uploads, ranked them by views, and ran the top videos through the Data Gatherer at one-second sampling. The analysis measured what that channel actually shows against what its narrator says, shot by shot. The findings became skill packs, the packs became a new channel, and a Wan style LoRA was trained on a curated, shot-aligned dataset to carry the look.

sections.heading: How a video gets made
sections.body:
The pipeline order is non-negotiable, and voice comes first.

- It starts with an idea typed into the channel's Autopilot box. A local LLM interprets it, researches the story (dates, people, reference photos), and writes the script against a strict spec: cold open under 12 words, context before event, one idea per scene, a curiosity gap that lives only in the title and hook.
- One-take narration: the entire script goes through Qwen3-TTS in a single pass, gets humanized (mic, room and pacing imperfections), then Whisper aligns every scene to the take and QA-checks the transcript against the script. Word-level timestamps become the clock for everything downstream.
- Every scene gets a still from krea2 via ComfyUI, composed under the channel's art direction. Hero scenes earn real Wan 2.2 14B motion clips, sharpened by Real-ESRGAN, each running as long as its scene stays on screen.
- The auto-director fills in what the writer didn't: transitions, shot variety, sound cues, and one word-synced emphasis per scene, all chosen from the effects grammar. Date stamps, name tags and evidence 'receipts' are typeset by Remotion, never drawn by the video model.
- A mood-matched instrumental bed is auto-scored under the voice. Assembly runs segmented and in parallel, the ending fades to black with the audio easing out, and a final ffmpeg color-grade pass (bloom, vignette, grain) goes over the finished file.
- Packaging writes research-driven SEO that quotes the video's own narration, renders thumbnail variants from typeset templates, cuts vertical Shorts at scene boundaries, and uploads private-first to the channel's YouTube account on a schedule, as a 1440p master so YouTube grants it a better bitrate tier. The publish page then shows the on-platform truth live: processing state, privacy, and whether the live title has drifted from the app's.

sections.heading: The system carries the intelligence
sections.body:
The design principle throughout: the pipeline must produce a competent video even when the writing model is small and local. Everything that can be decided deterministically is.

- One editable JSON dictionary, the effects grammar, maps narration beats (money, reveal, impact, motion) to the stinger, the transition, the shot rotation and the music mood. The director and the audio scorer both read it, so teaching the system a new reflex is a one-file edit, visible right in Settings.
- Safety and quality rules are enforced in code, not trust: a no-text negative prompt is force-appended to every render, a vision model inspects each clip for leaked glyphs and re-rolls the seed, and every figure must be explicitly clothed in the prompt.
- Per-video variance is engineered: direction cards bend each video's hook style and rhythm, thumbnail templates rotate so no two consecutive videos match, and title formulas rotate the same way. Same rules every time, different skeleton every video.

sections.heading: The hard part
sections.body:
- 16 GB of VRAM for TTS, image, video and music models meant strict orchestration: lazy loading, stage-by-stage frees during production, an idle reaper, and one queue everything must pass through.
- Beating the AI tells was an iteration loop with real stakes: watch the render, list every tell (an extra hand, a wrong reflection, a robotic ending, burned-in gibberish), then fix the system so that class of error can't recur. The rules file reads like a war journal.
- It survived a real data-loss incident: the channels folder was wiped outside the app. The scripts were recovered from session transcripts and, because every generated PNG and Wan clip embeds its own generation graph, 242 images and all 36 motion clips were recovered bit-for-bit from the render cache without a single GPU minute. The studio now git-tracks exactly what defines it.
